teaser: Software is now a product: the EU's new Product Liability Directive read article by article, applied to SaaS, updates and php2shell.
core_idea: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 makes software, including SaaS, a product under no-fault liability for products placed on the market after 9 December 2026, removes the later-defect defence for missing security updates within the maker's control, and ignores attackers and EULAs, but only natural persons can claim and only for injury, private property and private data destroyed, so for php2shell unpatched vendors and SaaS harming consumers are likely liable while leaks and business losses fall outside.

figures.caption: Lauren Zabierek's post on LinkedIn, 25 October 2026: a card, R-05, on the Product Liability Directive. The 1985 directive never named software; Directive 2024/2853 makes standalone software, SaaS, AI systems and digital manufacturing files products, subject to strict, no-fault liability; courts can presume defectiveness and causation where a defect is too complex to prove; the liability cannot be waived by a EULA; it applies to products placed on the EU market from 9 December 2026.

Does the new Product Liability Directive bite? Six questions, in order: is it a product (software is, including SaaS; services as such and mere source code are not); was it placed on the market after 9 December 2026; was it supplied in a commercial activity (non-commercial open source is excluded); is the injured person a natural person; is the damage covered (injury, private property, private data destroyed or corrupted); is the product defective (judged with safety-relevant cybersecurity requirements). Then the defences, and what is not a defence.

php2shell under the new directive: the PHP project, no, open source outside a commercial activity; a vendor shipping an appliance or app on unpatched PHP, likely, for a consumer's injury, property or personal data destroyed; a SaaS whose unpatched PHP lets attackers wipe or encrypt consumers' personal files, likely; the same SaaS if attackers only steal the data, not under this directive; a business that loses its own data, no claim under this directive; a product shipped on end-of-life PHP 7.4, hard to defend. A reading of the text, not legal advice.
